title: A Day Out in Vancouver
text:
I’d only been in Vancouver for a couple of weeks, so I decided to conduct a fairly ambitious experiment: how much of the city could I see in a single day?
The answer turned out to be quite a lot — although my feet had a different opinion by the end.
I somehow managed to fit a forest, an ocean, a skyline, and a pint of beer into one day, all before sunset.

title: A Day Out in Vancouver
text:
Stanley Park
First stop: Stanley Park.
I’d heard it was big, but walking into it still caught me off guard — massive trees on one side, the ocean on the other, and a seawall that just keeps going.
I spent the morning wandering the trails, half expecting to see a bear. I didn’t — thankfully, or unfortunately, depending on how brave I was feeling that day.






Tip



If you’re doing this in one day like I did, start at Stanley Park early. It’s very easy to lose track of time here.





View from Stanley Park


One of the things I liked most was how quickly the scenery changed. One minute I was surrounded by trees, and the next I was looking out over the water with downtown in the distance.
Having only recently moved here, it was one of those moments where Vancouver started to feel a little less like a place I’d moved to and a little more like a place I was beginning to know.

title: A Day Out in Vancouver
text:
Vancouver Aquarium
From the park, it was a short walk to the Vancouver Aquarium.
The sea otters were doing their absolute best to steal the show, and, frankly, they had no competition. I probably spent twenty minutes just watching them float around.
They appeared to have mastered the art of having absolutely nowhere else to be.
It’s a good reminder of how much marine life is sitting right off the coast here.



Otters at Stanley Park Aquarium

title: A Day Out in Vancouver
text:
Vancouver Lookout
By the afternoon, I made my way downtown to the Vancouver Lookout for a completely different perspective — literally.
Seeing the whole city laid out from up there, with the mountains in the background and the water on every side, made it click just how much Vancouver is shaped by its geography.
After seeing the city from ground level all morning, it was nice to finally see what all the walking had added up to.
Worth the elevator ride up.



View from Vancouver Lookout

title: A Day Out in Vancouver
text:
Gastown
By this point, I had walked enough that my feet had started submitting complaints.
So I ended the day exactly the way you’re supposed to end a good day of exploring: a beer in Gastown.
Cobblestone streets, the steam clock doing its thing, and a cold drink after a full day of walking — a solid way to close out my first real tour of the city.




Four stops, one day, and I think I understand Vancouver a little better now.
I’m still very new to the city, but one thing I’ve already noticed is how easy it is to go from forest to ocean to skyline to historic neighbourhood without really feeling like you’ve left the city at all.
There are still plenty of places I haven’t seen, which is probably a good thing.
My feet may disagree, but I think I’m going to like it here.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
My first week in MDS was quite interesting.
I had been preparing for this move for months. Then, quite suddenly, I was sitting on a plane at 3 in the morning wondering how exactly I had agreed to do this.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
The Flight



View from the Sky


I started my flight from India at 3 in the morning.
Twenty hours of travelling, a 4-hour layover in Frankfurt, and several attempts at sleeping later, I landed in Vancouver.
It was 3 in the afternoon.
Apparently, when you cross enough time zones, your birthday starts behaving like a distributed system.






Note



Longest birthday ever: Landing day happened to be my birthday. Crossing that many time zones gave me the longest birthday of my life.
At this point, I had been awake for approximately 47 years, although the exact number is still pending validation.


The slightly strange part was that despite leaving India at 3 AM and travelling for most of the day, Vancouver greeted me with another 3 PM.
My body, meanwhile, had stopped participating in the experiment.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
Jericho Beach
I stayed in a hostel near Jericho Beach for the first week.
This turned out to be an excellent decision.
I’m a big fan of beaches, so about ten minutes after checking in, I headed out to see it for myself.
I ended up standing there for a while, watching the waves wash over my feet with the evening sun coming down.



Jericho Beach


After spending roughly a day travelling halfway across the world, it was probably the first moment when it actually felt like:
Okay. I’m here.
And then I remembered I had to figure out where I was going to buy groceries.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
Orientation
The next day, I attended the MDS Orientation.
After travelling from India, waking up in a new country, and spending the previous day contemplating the meaning of time, suddenly being surrounded by a room full of people who were all about to spend the next year doing the same program was a little surreal.
I met a lot of new people, and one of the things I enjoyed most was hearing everyone’s stories — where they came from, what they had been doing before MDS, and what brought them here.
There was a surprisingly large amount of interesting life experience packed into one cohort.
I’m looking forward to getting to know everyone better over the next year.






Tip



Data Science lesson #1: Meeting an entire cohort at once produces a rather impressive amount of unstructured data.





Beer Night with New People

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
So far
One week in, and the experiment has started.
I’ve moved to a new country, started a new degree, met a lot of new people, found a beach within ten minutes of my hostel, and somehow managed to have a birthday that lasted significantly longer than intended.
Not a bad first week.
Now I just have to survive the rest of the program.
And Vancouver winter.
Those are two separate problems.

title: A Little Analysis with Python
text:
The following analysis comes from the IMDB dataset, which contains 1,000 movies from 2006–2016, along with information about their genre, rating, number of votes, revenue, and other attributes.
The columns in the dataset are:
Rank, Title, Genre, Description, Director, Actors, Year, Runtime (Minutes), Rating, Votes, Revenue (Millions), and Metascore.
The dataset is available here.
I’m going to look at two fairly simple questions:
Nothing particularly groundbreaking here. This is mostly an exercise in getting comfortable with pandas, manipulating the data into a form that is useful for analysis, and making plots that are actually readable.

title: A Little Analysis with Python

The dataset is already fairly analysis-friendly, but there is one slightly inconvenient column: Genre.
A movie can belong to multiple genres, so instead of having one genre per row, the dataset stores them together as a comma-separated string.
For example, a movie might be classified as:
Action, Adventure, Sci-Fi
That is fine for displaying the data, but not ideal if we want to compare ratings across genres. So the first thing we need to do is split those values apart.

title: A Little Analysis with Python
text:
Rating Distribution across Genres
Among the movies associated with each genre, how are their IMDB ratings distributed?

df['Genre'] = df['Genre'].str.split(',')
df_exploded = df.explode('Genre')
df_exploded['Genre'] = df_exploded['Genre'].str.strip()


genre_counts = df_exploded['Genre'].value_counts()
common_genres = genre_counts[genre_counts >= 10].index
df_common = df_exploded[df_exploded['Genre'].isin(common_genres)]

order = (
    df_common.groupby('Genre')['Rating']
    .median()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .index
)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
data_by_genre = [df_common[df_common['Genre'] == g]['Rating'].values for g in order]

plt.boxplot(data_by_genre, tick_labels=list(order), patch_artist=True,
            boxprops=dict(facecolor='steelblue', alpha=0.6))
plt.title('Distribution of IMDB Ratings by Genre')
plt.xlabel('Genre')
plt.ylabel('Rating')
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








There are a couple of things happening here that are worth pointing out.
First, I’m using a boxplot instead of simply calculating the average rating. An average would give us one number for each genre, but it wouldn’t tell us much about how those ratings are distributed.
The boxplot gives us a better idea of the median, the middle 50% of ratings, and the spread of the data. It also makes it easier to spot genres where a few movies have ratings that are quite different from the rest.
I also filtered out genres that appear fewer than 10 times in the dataset. There isn’t much value in comparing a genre represented by only a handful of movies against one represented by hundreds of movies. The cutoff of 10 is somewhat arbitrary, but it keeps the visualization focused on genres with at least a reasonable number of observations.
The plot also makes the variation within genres more interesting than simply comparing their medians. Some genres have a relatively tight distribution of ratings, while others have movies spread across a much wider range.
So, rather than trying to declare a single “best” genre from this plot, I’d treat it as a way of seeing how different genres are represented in this particular IMDB dataset.

title: A Little Analysis with Python
section: Top Grossing Movies across each Year
text:
Top Grossing Movies across each Year
For each year, which movie had the highest reported revenue?
There is one complication here: some movies don’t have a value recorded for Revenue (Millions). Since we can’t identify the highest-grossing movie from a missing value, those rows need to be excluded from this particular analysis.

df_rev = df.dropna(subset=['Revenue (Millions)'])

idx = df_rev.groupby('Year')['Revenue (Millions)'].idxmax()
top_per_year = df_rev.loc[idx].sort_values('Year')


plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.plot(top_per_year['Year'], top_per_year['Revenue (Millions)'],
         marker='o', color='steelblue', linewidth=2)

# Annotate each point with the movie title
for _, row in top_per_year.iterrows():
    plt.annotate(row['Title'],
                 (row['Year'], row['Revenue (Millions)']),
                 textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 8),
                 fontsize=7, rotation=30, ha='left')

plt.title('Highest-Grossing Movie by Year')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Revenue (Millions USD)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








I like this visualization a little more than a simple table because the year-to-year changes become much easier to see.
There are some fairly dramatic jumps in the revenue of the highest-grossing movie from one year to another. A single blockbuster can pull the top of the chart considerably higher, so the line isn’t really showing a smooth trend in the movie industry. It’s showing how the biggest hit in the dataset changed from year to year.
The movie titles are also useful here. Without them, we’d just have a line moving up and down with no idea what caused each point.
One thing that stands out is how much the biggest movies can dominate the numbers. A year with one enormous franchise release can look very different from a year where the highest-grossing movie had a much smaller box office.

title: A Little Analysis with Python
section: A few things I took away
text:
A few things I took away
This was a relatively simple analysis, but there were a few useful pandas lessons hiding inside it.
The first was explode(). Whenever a column contains multiple values packed into a single cell, it can be useful to turn those values into separate rows before doing any grouping or aggregation.
The second was the importance of looking at the distribution, rather than immediately reducing everything to an average. The genre analysis is much more informative as a boxplot because we can see variation between movies, not just one summary statistic.
And finally, there is the slightly less exciting but probably more important part of data analysis: being careful about what the data actually represents.
It’s easy to look at a chart and come away with a strong conclusion. But in this case, we’re working with a curated dataset, movies can belong to multiple genres, and some revenue values are missing. Those details don’t make the analysis useless; they just determine what conclusions we can reasonably draw from it.
Which is probably a good reminder that the hardest part of data analysis isn’t always writing the code.
Sometimes it’s deciding what the code is actually telling you.

title: A Little Analysis with R
text:
The following analysis comes from the IMDB dataset, which contains 1,000 movies from 2006–2016, along with information about their genre, rating, number of votes, revenue, and other attributes.
The columns in the dataset are:
Rank, Title, Genre, Description, Director, Actors, Year, Runtime (Minutes), Rating, Votes, Revenue (Millions), and Metascore.
The dataset is available here.
I’m going to look at two fairly simple questions:
Nothing particularly groundbreaking here. This is mostly an excuse to spend some time with R and the tidyverse, and to see how some of the same ideas I would normally reach for in Python translate into R.

title: A Little Analysis with R
text:
Data Reading
We can start by reading the data using the pandas library:

library(tidyverse)

The dataset is already in a fairly convenient format, so there isn’t a huge amount of cleaning required.
The one column that needs a little attention is Genre.
A movie can belong to more than one genre, so instead of having a single value like Drama, we might have something like Action, Adventure, Sci-Fi sitting inside one cell.
That’s perfectly reasonable for a dataset intended for browsing, but it becomes slightly inconvenient when we want to group movies by genre.
So let’s separate those values first.

title: A Little Analysis with R
text:
Runtime Distribution across Genres
Are some types of movies generally longer than others?

df_long <- df |>
  separate_rows(Genre, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(Genre = str_trim(Genre))

genre_counts <- df_long |> count(Genre)
common_genres <- genre_counts |> filter(n >= 10) |> pull(Genre)

df_common <- df_long |> filter(Genre %in% common_genres)

genre_order <- df_common |>
  group_by(Genre) |>
  summarise(median_runtime = median(`Runtime (Minutes)`, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(median_runtime)) |>
  pull(Genre)

df_common <- df_common |>
  mutate(Genre = factor(Genre, levels = genre_order))


ggplot(df_common, aes(x = Genre, y = `Runtime (Minutes)`, fill = Genre)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Runtime by Genre",
       x = "Genre", y = "Runtime (Minutes)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The first thing I wanted to look at was runtime.
Rather than just calculating the average runtime for each genre, I’m using a boxplot. This gives us a little more information about the distribution of runtimes within each genre.
The ordering is based on the median runtime, so the genres at the top of the chart have the highest typical runtime in this dataset.
I also filtered out genres with fewer than 10 movies. There isn’t much point in making strong visual comparisons for a genre represented by only a handful of observations.
The interesting part of the plot isn’t necessarily which genre has the single longest runtime. It’s the spread within each genre.
Some genres have a fairly compact range of runtimes, while others have movies scattered across a much wider range. The median gives us one way of comparing the typical movie, while the boxplot shows us how much variation exists around that typical value.
So this plot gives us a useful overview of how runtime varies across the genres represented in the dataset, without pretending that runtime alone tells us anything particularly profound about a movie.

title: A Little Analysis with R
section: Top Rated Movies across each Year
text:
Top Rated Movies across each Year
Now let’s look at ratings.
Instead of asking which genre has the highest rating, I’m going to change the question slightly:
For each year, which movie had the highest IMDB rating?

top_per_year <- df |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  slice_max(order_by = Rating, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(Year)

top_per_year |> select(Year, Title, Rating)

# A tibble: 11 × 3
    Year Title                   Rating
   <dbl> <chr>                    <dbl>
 1  2006 The Prestige               8.5
 2  2007 Taare Zameen Par           8.5
 3  2008 The Dark Knight            9  
 4  2009 3 Idiots                   8.4
 5  2010 Inception                  8.8
 6  2011 The Intouchables           8.6
 7  2012 The Dark Knight Rises      8.5
 8  2013 The Wolf of Wall Street    8.2
 9  2014 Interstellar               8.6
10  2015 Bahubali: The Beginning    8.3
11  2016 Dangal                     8.8

ggplot(top_per_year, aes(x = Year, y = Rating)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Title), angle = 30, hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5,
            size = 2.5, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Highest-Rated Movie by Year",
       x = "Year", y = "Rating") +
  theme_minimal()








This one is a little more straightforward.
group_by(Year) lets us consider each year separately, and slice_max() then picks the movie with the highest rating within that year.
I used with_ties = FALSE here so that we get exactly one movie per year, even if two movies happen to have the same rating.
The resulting table is useful on its own, but the plot makes the year-to-year pattern easier to see.
The line isn’t really showing a trend in movie quality. It’s showing the maximum rating among the movies present in this dataset for each year.
That’s an important distinction.
We’re not looking at every movie released in each year, and we’re certainly not measuring the quality of an entire year’s movies. We’re just asking which movie in this particular dataset had the highest rating for that year.
The labels make the chart a little more interesting because we can connect the numbers back to actual movies. Otherwise we’d just have a line moving between ratings without much context.
It’s also worth remembering that the difference between, say, an 8.1 and an 8.2 isn’t necessarily meaningful by itself. Ratings are aggregates, and the number of votes, audience composition, and other factors can all affect them.
Still, as a small exploratory exercise, it’s a nice way of combining grouping, filtering, and visualization.

title: A Little Analysis with R
section: A few things I took away
text:
A few things I took away
The main reason for doing this analysis wasn’t really to discover some profound fact about movies.
It was to get more comfortable with R.
Coming from Python, some of the ideas feel immediately familiar. group_by() and summarise() cover much of the same territory as pandas’ grouping operations, while ggplot2 provides a very different but surprisingly intuitive way of thinking about visualizations.
The biggest difference I noticed was how naturally the tidyverse encourages you to think about data as a sequence of transformations:
take the data → transform it → group it → summarize it → visualize it.
Once the syntax starts becoming familiar, the individual operations aren’t particularly complicated.
The more interesting part, as usual, is deciding what the resulting numbers actually mean.
For example, the genre analysis isn’t really telling us that one genre causes longer movies, and the yearly rating analysis isn’t telling us which year produced the “best” movies.
They’re just two different ways of looking at the same dataset.
And honestly, that’s probably a good enough reason to spend an afternoon playing around with it.

title: About
text:
I grew up in Mysore, India, where I developed an appreciation for good food, travel, and probably an unhealthy attachment to Mysore Pak.



I studied Electrical Engineering at PES University in Bangalore.



After graduating, I spent five years at Bosch as a Senior ML Engineer, working on anomaly detection, computer vision, and NLP.
Five years of teaching machines to detect unusual things seemed like a reasonable amount of time to spend thinking about what I wanted to do next.



I decided to continue my studies and moved to Canada to start the Master of Data Science at UBC.
So, after five years of industry experience, I voluntarily went back to school.
This seemed like a good idea at the time.

title: About
text:
Why data science
I was inspired by projects such as Project Euphonia, Project Relate, and Project Lookout.



What I find particularly interesting about these projects is that the technology isn’t the end goal. The goal is to help people communicate, move, and live more independently.
That’s the kind of ML work I want to keep doing.
Accessibility is the thread that runs through most of the problems I want to work on: using technology to make everyday systems more useful and inclusive for more people.

text:
When I’m not doing ML

🌍 Travel
I love travelling and exploring new places. I’m particularly interested in experiencing a place rather than simply checking its landmarks off a list.
Getting lost somewhere interesting is generally preferable to following a perfectly optimized itinerary.


🍜 Food
I like trying new restaurants and exploring different cuisines.
I consider this research.
The methodology is mostly eating.


🎸 Guitar
I’m currently learning to play guitar.
Progress so far: enough to make the neighbours aware that I am learning guitar.
The long-term objective is to eventually produce something that sounds intentional.


🏖️ Vancouver
I’ve only recently moved to Vancouver, but the combination of mountains, ocean, beaches, and city life has made it a pretty easy place to like.
I’m also still collecting evidence on whether I can survive the weather.
